prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: Document ingestion environment variables (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Name" · longest unbreakable unit 377px · widest one-line content 377px
  col 2: header "Required" · longest unbreakable unit 78px · widest one-line content 78px
  col 3: header "Default" · longest unbreakable unit 169px · widest one-line content 169px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable unit 172px · widest one-line content 1212px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 720px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). At 720px some words cannot fit unsplit. Horizontal scrolling is ALLOWED: the table may be wider than 720px (column widths summing to more than 719px) (the reader scrolls), or you may fit within 719px and accept the consequences. Fitting and scrolling layouts are judged as two separate classes; propose good layouts of BOTH kinds.
Rendering convention: a full render shows the WHOLE table; anything right of the dashed box is not clipped — it is reached by scrolling. Where a layout scrolls, an extra "viewport view" image shows only what is visible at first sight.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Help readers configure document ingestion by finding each environment variable, its requirement, default value, and operational meaning.","tasks":["Look up a variable by its exact name and read across its row.","Compare which variables are required and what defaults they use.","Read descriptions to understand behavior, dependencies, and configuration consequences."],"relations":["Each variable name identifies the requirement, default, and description in the same row.","Conditional requirements and operational cautions are explained in the description and must remain easy to associate with their variable."],"roles":["Name cells are row headers and the primary lookup anchors.","Required and Default are compact comparison columns.","Description carries the explanatory prose and needs the most flexible reading measure."],"keep_whole":["Environment variable names, including identifiers embedded in descriptions, should ideally remain intact.","Requirement values, numeric defaults, and the default URL should ideally remain intact."],"may_wrap":["Descriptions may wrap at natural word boundaries.","In a viewport-fitting layout, long identifiers and the URL may need to break within the cell."],"same_scale":["All row headers should use one consistent column width.","Required and Default both contain short lookup values, but Default needs more space for the URL.","Descriptions share one width even though their lengths vary."],"h_vs_v":"Fitting the viewport avoids horizontal scrolling but forces breaks in long identifiers or the URL and produces taller rows. Scrolling can preserve lookup values and give descriptions a more comfortable measure, at the cost of hiding some columns on first sight."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d1r0A, d1r0B (full view, then viewport view), d1r0C (full view, then viewport view).
Measured facts:
d1r0A: column widths [260, 99, 120, 240] px · table 720×1035 px · row heights [36, 176, 129, 129, 129, 153, 129, 153] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 7 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 6 · fits the 720 px viewport (no scrolling)
d1r0B: column widths [398, 99, 190, 360] px · table 1048×710 px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 83, 83, 106, 83, 106] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 328 px (horizontal scrolling)
d1r0C: column widths [398, 99, 190, 650] px · table 1338×454 px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0 · WIDER than the viewport by 618 px (horizontal scrolling)

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). This is your first look at real renders: propose at least one improved or alternative design (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or test an important idea you have not tried). "done" is not allowed yet. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
